title: Government remains committed to ensuring that children are able to benefit from digital technologies while being protected from online harms
body_text:
The Government recognizes the transformative potential of emerging digital technologies, particularly in enhancing access to education, information and services for children. At the same time, the Government is cognizant of the associated risks, including exposure to harmful content, cyberbullying, online abuse, excessive screen time and digital dependency, thereby necessitating appropriate safeguards for children in the digital environment.
The Government has put in place a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework under the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (as amended), and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 to ensure a safe, secure and accountable online environment for users, including children.
The Information Technology Act, 2000, read with the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, provides a comprehensive legal framework to ensure a safe and accountable online environment. The Rules mandate intermediaries to exercise due diligence and prohibit hosting or transmission of unlawful content, including content that is obscene, pornographic, invasive of privacy, harmful to children, promotes hate or violence, impersonates individuals, or threatens public order.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 further provides safeguards for children by requiring verifiable consent of parents or lawful guardians prior to processing of their personal data and prohibits practices such as tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. The DPDP Rules prescribe operational mechanisms for obtaining verifiable parental consent, including through identity and age verification measures and the use of virtual tokens. It also provides for the right to withdraw consent, with corresponding obligations on data fiduciaries to erase such data in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has established the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) to provide a framework and eco-system for Law Enforcement Agencies to deal with cyber-crimes in a comprehensive and coordinated Manner. The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (https://cybercrime.gov.in) enables the public to report all types of cybercrimes, with special emphasis on crimes against children. To strengthen a comprehensive and coordinated response mechanism to deal with cybercrimes, the Central Government has implemented measures such as raising public awareness, issuing alerts and advisories, training LEA personnel, prosecutors and judicial officers, and upgrading cyber forensic facilities.
The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) has developed several resources to promote online safety. These include the “Being Safe Online” guidelines for awareness among children, parents, educators and the public; the Manual on Safety and Security of Children in Schools incorporating guidelines for prevention of cyberbullying; and the Guidelines on Preventing Cyber Bullying for school children issued in 2024. These resources provide information regarding online safety, reporting mechanisms, preventive measures and responsible online behaviour.
During 2025-26, NCPCR conducted conferences at State and district levels across the country on child rights issues, including school safety and cyber safety, and organised capacity-building programmes for school administrators and educators on child protection laws and safety practices. NCPCR is also conducting virtual district workshops on school safety and child security.
National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) commissioned a national level study on “Effects (Physical, Behavioural and Psycho- social) of using mobile phones and other devices with internet accessibility by children” in 2021. The main objective of the study was to understand physical, behavioural, and psycho-social effects on children of using mobile phones and other devices with internet accessibility. This was a nationwide study of all regions. The total number of responses collected were of 5,811 participants, consisting of 3,491 school going children, 1,534 parents and 786 teachers from 60 schools, across six states in the country. The study report is available on NCPCR’s website at-
https://ncpcr.gov.in/public/viewPdf/165650458362bc410794e02_effect1.PDF
The Ministry of Education issued the PRAGYATA Guidelines on Digital Education in July 2020, which provide a framework for safe and effective online learning, including promotion of students’ well-being and responsible use of social media and electronic devices. CBSE has supplemented these efforts through guidelines on digital etiquette, cybersecurity training for teachers, publication of the Cyber Security Handbook and advisories to schools for establishing Cyber Clubs to promote cyber safety awareness. NCERT has also incorporated cyber safety in its curriculum and developed resource materials on cyber safety and security.
The Government remains committed to ensuring that children are able to benefit from digital technologies while being protected from online harms.
This information was given by the Minister of State for Women and Child Development Smt. Savitri Thakur in Rajya Sabha in reply to a question.

ministry.name: Ministry of Women and Child Development

enrichment.summary: In a Rajya Sabha reply, the Ministry of Women and Child Development outlined the government's multi-pronged framework to protect children online while enabling digital access to education and services. This includes the IT Act 2000, IT Intermediary Guidelines 2021, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, I4C's cybercrime reporting portal, and NCPCR initiatives like 'Being Safe Online' guidelines and a 2021 study on mobile/internet effects on children covering 5,811 respondents across six states. Education Ministry bodies (CBSE, NCERT) have also integrated cyber safety into curricula and teacher training.
enrichment.context:
Child online safety has become a pressing policy concern globally as internet penetration among minors rises sharply in India, alongside risks like cyberbullying, grooming, and data exploitation. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is a landmark law that, for the first time, codifies statutory protections for children's data, mandating verifiable parental consent and banning behavioural tracking and targeted ads aimed at minors—provisions still being operationalized through draft DPDP Rules. This complements the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which impose due-diligence obligations on platforms to remove unlawful or harmful content.

Institutionally, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) under MHA and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal represent India's coordinated law-enforcement response to cybercrime, including crimes against children, while the NCPCR (a statutory body under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005) plays a child-rights watchdog and awareness-building role. The Ministry of Education's PRAGYATA Guidelines (2020), issued during the COVID-19 pandemic to regulate online schooling, remain a reference framework for balancing digital learning with student well-being. Together these measures reflect India's evolving regulatory architecture at the intersection of child rights, data privacy, and digital governance—an area of growing legislative and judicial attention worldwide.

prelims_questions.question: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 mandates which of the following with respect to processing of children's personal data?
options: Automatic consent once a child registers an email ID
Verifiable consent of parents or lawful guardians before processing
Consent only required for children below 10 years of age
No restriction on behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that the DPDP Act, 2023 requires verifiable consent of parents or lawful guardians prior to processing children's personal data and prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring, and targeted advertising directed at children.

prelims_questions.question: Which organization operates the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal mentioned in relation to child protection?
options: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR)
Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) under the Ministry of Home Affairs
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology directly
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that the Ministry of Home Affairs established I4C, which enables the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) for reporting cybercrimes, including crimes against children.
